claim: The Geneplore model splits creative work into a generate phase that builds rough pre-inventive structures and an explore phase that tests and develops them, and the two phases cycle.
quote: generate stage produces rough early ideas, which the authors call pre-inventive structures
title: Creative Cognition: Theory, Research, and Applications
transfer: Two alternating calls: GENERATE makes many rough candidate seeds with no judging; EXPLORE interprets each seed, tries to make it fit a goal, and keeps or drops it. Loop until a seed survives. Book itself not opened; description comes from a search summary.

claim: Finke's experiments with parts of 3D shapes showed that people can build useful inventions from random pre-inventive parts if they are asked to interpret them afterward, supporting generate-then-interpret.
quote: Finke's 1990 experiments with 3D shapes, which were rated for creativity, provide some supporting evidence.
title: Creative Cognition (Geneplore description)
transfer: Give the model random or forced parts first (random object, random constraint), then require it to find a use or meaning. Interpretation after random generation is a legitimate step, not a trick. Effect sizes not found; re-check Finke 1990 if used.

claim: When asked to imagine novel category members (alien animals, fruit, tools), people take a path of least resistance: they recall a known earth exemplar and modify it, so most inventions keep typical properties such as bilateral symmetry, sense organs and limbs.
quote: the majority of imagined creatures were structured by properties that are typical animals on earth: bilateral symmetry, sensory receptors, and appendages.
title: Structured imagination: The role of category structure in exemplar generation
transfer: Default generation by an LLM is the same: it retrieves a prototype and edits it. Add a step that lists the typical properties of the category first, then forbids or varies the ones the first draft kept. Paper not opened; wording comes from a search summary of later papers.

claim: The path-of-least-resistance idea is still used in 2021 work: avoiding it requires changing one's mental representation to subvert salient conceptual knowledge, and it is said to be shown across animals, tools, fruit and toys.
quote: avoiding the path of least resistance by changing one's mental representations of label-figure pairs to subvert salient conceptual knowledge
title: Neural Representations of Conceptual Fixation during Creative Imagination
transfer: Supports a 'break the representation' step: ask the model to restate the problem object with its most salient property removed, then generate again.

claim: Showing example designs makes people copy their features (design fixation); the effect appears in engineering students and professionals, and in lab tasks.
quote: Engineering design students and professionals who saw example designs were significantly more likely to conform to them than those who did not.
authors: Jansson & Smith (1991), as summarized by Chrysikou et al.
title: Design fixation (summary in Functional Fixedness in Creative Thinking Tasks Depends on Stimulus Modality)
transfer: Do not put the model's own first answers or prior examples into the context of the next generation call. Generate in parallel from a clean prompt; show examples only after, to the judge.

claim: Participants copy features of examples even after a distractor task and even when told to avoid the examples.
quote: Participants who saw pictorial examples tended to conform to them, even after a distractor task or an instruction to avoid the examples.
authors: Smith, Ward, Schumacher (1993), as summarized by Chrysikou et al.
title: Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
transfer: An instruction like 'do not repeat the earlier ideas' is weak. Remove earlier ideas from the context instead, or filter duplicates with code after generation.

claim: A 2022 paper states that copying of example features has been observed even when people are told to avoid it or are shown flawed examples, across alien creatures, toys and cups.
quote: Reproducing concrete attributes of example images has also been observed even when participants are explicitly instructed to avoid replicating exemplar components or are shown flawed, incorrect examples
title: Neural Representations of Conceptual Fixation during Creative Imagination
transfer: Same as a-06; independent restatement in a recent paper, so the finding is not only the 1993 study.

claim: A meta-analytic review of examples in design ideation (Sio, Kotovsky, Cagan) reports examples can reduce idea fluency and fixate, though they can also inspire; the conditions matter.
quote: Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
title: Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
transfer: Examples are a lever with a sign that depends on timing and distance. Test both in our loop: far examples after a first free pass versus none. Effect sizes not retrieved; open the paper before using numbers.

claim: Across 22 experiments comparing real brainstorming groups with nominal groups (same people working alone, pooled), 18 found nominal groups better and 4 found no difference; none found real groups better.
quote: the 22 experiments listed in Table 1, 18 reported the performance of nominal groups to be superior to that of real groups, and only 4, all involving 2-person groups
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: For an LLM, independent parallel samples then pooling is the nominal group. Do not make samples talk to each other during generation; combine after.

claim: Production blocking (waiting for your turn so ideas are forgotten or suppressed) accounted for most of the productivity loss in real brainstorming groups, not free riding or fear of evaluation.
quote: production blocking accounted for most of the productivity loss of real brainstorming groups
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: Let each generator finish its own list before any reading of others. Sequential multi-agent dialogue is a blocking design; avoid it for the generate phase.

claim: Inducing evaluation apprehension reduced productivity in individual brainstorming, but it did not explain the group-versus-nominal gap.
quote: inducing evaluation apprehension reduced productivity in individual brainstorming
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: Judging during generation costs ideas. Keep generation and evaluation in separate calls, as Geneplore and Osborn's rule both say.

claim: The meta-analysis of brainstorming groups found nominal groups generally better, with the loss larger for bigger groups.
quote: Nominal groups are generally better
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: A meta-analytic integration
n: not found; effect sizes not retrieved
transfer: Pooling many independent lists beats a talking group, and the cost of talking grows with group size. Quote is from a third-party summary page, not the paper (publisher page returned 403).

claim: Incubation (setting a problem aside, then returning) has a small positive average effect on problem solving: weighted mean unbiased effect size 0.29, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.39, over 117 effect sizes.
quote: The mean of the weighted unbiased effect size was 0.29, with a standard deviation of 0.04, and the 95% confidence interval was 0.21, 0.39.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: A cheap step: after a first failed or stale pass, drop the working draft, do an unrelated light task or a fresh restart, then retry. An LLM has no unconscious work, so the benefit would come only from clearing fixation; test it, do not assume it.

claim: Incubation helped divergent thinking tasks more than linguistic or visual insight tasks; longer preparation gave larger effects; filling the break with a demanding task shrank the effect.
quote: divergent thinking tasks benefiting more than linguistic and visual insight tasks from incubation. Longer preparation periods gave a greater incubation effect
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: Matches our own result pattern: restart or divergence pays on open tasks, little on single-answer tasks. Require real attempt effort before any restart (preparation), and restart only on open or stuck problems.

claim: Across 332 effect sizes, creativity enhancement methods raised creativity by Hedges g = 0.53 on average; the most effective were complex training courses, meditation and cultural exposure (g = 0.66); cognitive-manipulation drugs did nothing (g = 0.10).
quote: on average, creativity can be enhanced, Hedges' g = 0.53, 95%-CI [0.44, 0.61]
title: Creativity Enhancement Methods for Adults: A Meta-Analysis
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts (accepted version, preprint copy read)
transfer: Human training effects are moderate. They do not tell us what prompts do to an LLM; use only as a prior that structured idea techniques help somewhat.

claim: Haase et al. found methods aimed at convergent thinking worked better than methods aimed at divergent thinking, with a huge spread, and figural methods (g = 0.76) worked better than others.
quote: convergent thinking methods were more effective (g = 1.23, SE = 0.249, 95%-CI [0.14, 2.32], p < .0001, k = 11)
title: Creativity Enhancement Methods for Adults: A Meta-Analysis
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts (accepted version)
transfer: Only 11 effect sizes with an interval from 0.14 to 2.32 and a prediction interval of -1.92 to 4.38, so treat as weak. Suggests the select/converge half deserves as much design as the diverge half.

claim: A larger 2024 meta-analysis (169 studies, 844 effect sizes) found a raw training effect of 0.53 SD but strong signs of publication bias; adjusted estimates were only 0.29 to 0.32 SD, and many studies had method flaws.
quote: All adjustment methods considerably lowered our original estimate (adjusted estimates ranged from 0.29 to 0.32 SDs).
title: The impact of creativity training on creative performance: a meta-analytic review and critical evaluation of 5 decades of creativity training studies
transfer: Discount all creativity-technique effect sizes by about 40 percent and demand our own controlled test at equal tokens before keeping any step. It also contradicts the no-bias claim of a-15; the 2024 paper is the more careful one.

claim: Scott, Leritz and Mumford's review of about 70 creativity training studies reported an average effect of d = 0.64 and said good programs teach discrete cognitive skills with heuristics and practice in the domain.
quote: a review of 70 studies (Scott, Leritz & Mumford, 2004a, 2004b) concluded that training could indeed enhance creativity, with an average effect size d = 0.64.
authors: Scott, Leritz, Mumford (reported by a later review)
title: The effectiveness of creativity training: A quantitative review
transfer: Same ceiling caveat as a-17: 0.64 is pre-bias-correction. Useful design hint: teach specific skills (problem finding, combining concepts) rather than a general 'be creative' instruction. Second-hand figure; original paper not opened.

claim: Mednick's theory says highly creative people have flat associative hierarchies (many weak associations to a concept) and uncreative people steep ones (few strong ones); this was later questioned.
quote: higher creative individuals are characterized by "flat" associative hierarchies, with numerous and weakly related associations to a given concept
authors: Mednick (1962); Benedek & Neubauer (2013) questioned; as summarized in a search result for Beaty et al.
title: The roles of associative and executive processes in creative cognition
venue: Memory & Cognition 42(7), 1186-1197 (Beaty, Silvia, Nusbaum, Jauk, Benedek)
transfer: Beaty et al. found both associative and executive control matter for divergent thinking. For an agent: a step that widens retrieval (remote prompts) paired with a separate controlled filter. Not opened beyond a search summary.

claim: The Remote Associates Test asks for a single word that links three unrelated words (for example print, berry, bird -> blue), so it measures convergent, single-answer association.
quote: requires identifying a common associate that links a triad of words (e.g., print, berry,
title: Neural Representations of Conceptual Fixation during Creative Imagination
transfer: RAT-type items are single-answer, where our data says plain first answers win. Use for the checkable branch: generate several linking words, verify each against all three cues by code or lookup, never by vote.
